q: A summer day in the Cromwell basin can pass thirty degrees while the night that follows falls towards five. What does that swing give the region's Pinot Noir?
opts: A pale colour with almost no tannin at all
Green herbaceous flavours that never quite ripen out
Very high alcohol and a soft low-acid texture
Deep colour and ripe tannin, with acidity intact
exp: Ripening is driven by daytime warmth while acid is burned away through warm nights, so a wide daily range lets the two be pulled apart. It is the same mechanism that makes high-altitude vineyards work in hot countries, produced here by distance from the sea instead of by height.

q: Gold miners planted the first Central Otago vines in the 1860s, after which the district went most of a century without commercial wine. When did the modern revival take hold?
exp: Experimental blocks went in through the 1970s and the first commercial releases followed in the 1980s, once it was clear that Pinot Noir could ripen somewhere this extreme. Growth since has been rapid, and Pinot Noir now accounts for the great bulk of everything planted there.

q: French missionaries needing altar wine founded New Zealand's oldest surviving winery in 1851. In which region does it still stand?
exp: The Marist brothers settled on the east coast of the North Island and have made wine there ever since, which makes Hawke's Bay the oldest wine region of consequence in the country. It is also the second most planted, behind Marlborough and well ahead of everywhere else.

q: A flood in 1867 shifted a Hawke's Bay river off its course and left a bed of bare grey stones that farmers wrote off as worthless. What stands on that ground now?
exp: The Ngaruroro River abandoned the bed, and the shingle was quarried for road metal long before anyone thought to plant it. It is now the most closely watched red wine ground in New Zealand, given over to Bordeaux varieties and Syrah, with the Bridge Pa Triangle its near neighbour on deeper soils.

q: No government committee drew the boundary of the Gimblett Gravels, and no parish or council line marks it out. What fixes it instead?
opts: A minimum height above sea level written into the rules
A ten-kilometre radius drawn from the centre of Hastings
The extent of a single soil type, so the district stops where the gravels stop
The land held by the growers who founded the association, wherever it lies
exp: The boundary was traced from the soil survey, and the name itself is protected as a trademark held by the growers' association. A wine may carry it only if the overwhelming majority of its fruit was grown inside that soil line, which is an unusually strict rule for a New World appellation.

q: Bare stones across a vineyard floor soak up the day's heat and hand it back after sundown. Which grape does that most obviously rescue in Hawke's Bay?
exp: Cabernet ripens late and fails almost everywhere else in New Zealand, arriving green, hard and hollow. The stored warmth of the gravels supplies just enough extra heat at the end of the season to carry it home, which is why most of the country's serious Cabernet blends come from this stretch of ground, with Waiheke Island the only real rival.

q: Black pepper, violets and a medium body rather than jam and sweetness: Hawke's Bay has built an international reputation on one Rhone red. Which?
exp: Picked in a cool maritime autumn the grape keeps its peppery, floral register and lands nearer the northern Rhone than South Australia. New Zealand producers almost always print Syrah rather than Shiraz, and the choice of word is a deliberate statement about what is in the bottle.

q: Ordering the classic Hawke's Bay red, a guest is handed a blend rather than a single varietal wine. Which grapes are in the bottle?
opts: Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc and Malbec
Pinot Noir, Pinot Meunier and Gamay
Syrah, Grenache, Mourvedre, Carignan and Cinsault
exp: Merlot leads most of these blends because it ripens more dependably than Cabernet Sauvignon in a maritime autumn, with Cabernet Franc and Malbec adding perfume and colour. The model is the Right Bank of Bordeaux rather than the Medoc, even on the warmest gravels.

q: Wind funnels through a gap in the ranges and hammers Martinborough's vines through flowering every spring. What does that battering do to the wine?
opts: It strips acidity out of the fruit, giving soft early-drinking wine
It cuts the crop and thickens the skins, giving concentrated wine
It delays ripening so far that the fruit has to be picked green
It spreads botrytis through the canopy, so most fruit is picked sweet
exp: Wind at flowering knocks off potential berries before they ever set, and continued exposure leaves the vine with smaller fruit and thicker skins. That is why Martinborough makes so little wine, and why what it does make is denser than the size of the district would suggest.

q: Martinborough, Gladstone and Masterton all sit inside one registered region at the bottom of the North Island. What is that region called?
exp: Wairarapa is the official name and Martinborough the sub-district that made it famous, an hour or so over the hill from Wellington. It is among the smallest producing regions in the country by volume and among the most highly regarded by reputation.

q: Shielded from the prevailing westerlies by the Tararua Ranges, Martinborough stays markedly drier through autumn than Wellington an hour away. Why does that dryness matter so much to its Pinot Noir?
opts: Fruit can be left hanging to ripen fully without rot
It removes any need to prune the vine or manage its canopy
It guarantees the botrytis the district's sweet wines depend on
It concentrates sugar so far that chaptalisation becomes compulsory
exp: Pinot Noir has thin skins and tight bunches and rots readily in a wet autumn, and late rain swells the berries and dilutes what is in them, so how long a region dares leave fruit on the vine decides how ripe its tannin gets. For this grape a dry autumn is worth more than a warm summer.

q: Fertile alluvial flats on the east coast of the North Island, warm and humid with autumn rain a real risk, and a long-standing claim to be the country's Chardonnay capital. Which region?
exp: Gisborne is warm enough to ripen easily and fertile enough to crop heavily, which pushed it toward volume for most of its history. Its Chardonnay is broad and tropical rather than tight and mineral, and Gewurztraminer and Pinot Gris do well on the same flats.

q: An island in the harbour off New Zealand's largest city runs warmer and drier than the mainland beside it, and its growers plant Bordeaux reds and Syrah rather than Pinot Noir. Which island?
exp: Waiheke sits in the Hauraki Gulf a short ferry ride from Auckland, in a partial rain shadow with sea on every side holding off both frost and extreme heat. Land there is scarce and expensive, so the wines are made in small quantities and priced accordingly.

q: Croatian families who came to dig kauri gum in the nineteenth century planted vines west of Auckland, and their surnames are still on labels there. Which white grape is that district best known for now?
exp: The Dalmatian settlers stayed on, and their descendants founded several of the country's oldest wine companies, most of which still keep their head offices around Auckland. Kumeu, north-west of the city, has become New Zealand's benchmark address for tightly built barrel-fermented Chardonnay grown on heavy clay.

q: The first grapevines planted in New Zealand went into the ground in the far north in 1819. Who put them there?
exp: Marsden planted at Kerikeri in the Bay of Islands and left no record of any wine being made from the fruit. Busby, who arrived later and planted at Waitangi, is credited with the first recorded New Zealand wine, which a visiting French navigator tasted and praised around 1840.

q: One black grape covers more New Zealand ground than every other red variety put together, and it succeeds on river gravel, hillside clay and glacial schist alike. Which?
exp: Pinot Noir wants a long cool ripening season and a dry autumn, and most of the country offers exactly that. A great deal of the crop never appears as a red at all, because it also underpins the traditional-method sparkling wines.
